title: Baseline
tagline: Tennis ratings that publish a prediction **before** each match, then show you whether it was right.
role: Solo — data pipeline, API, and web app

hero.alt: The Baseline form board, listing players ranked by how far they are beating their own expected results
hero.caption: The form board ranks players by how far they are beating their own expected results — not by rating.

problem: Official tennis rankings measure points accumulated over a season. That is a fair way to seed a draw, but it answers the wrong question if you want to know who is playing well *now*: a player can hold a high ranking on results from eleven months ago, and a player beating people far above them climbs slowly.

I wanted to measure something rankings cannot express — form against expectation, adjusted for who a player actually faced — and to show the evidence behind every claim rather than asking anyone to trust a number.
data: 1.17 million ATP and WTA matches going back to 1968, plus rankings and, where they exist, serve and return statistics.

Two limits are properties of the data and appear in the interface rather than in a footnote: WTA results stop at 16 December 2024 while ATP runs to 28 April 2026, and serve/return statistics only start in 1991 for ATP and 2006 for WTA. The source repositories were deleted in mid-2026, so the pipeline now recovers them from the Software Heritage archive.
built: A pipeline that downloads and ingests the raw sources into DuckDB, reshapes them into a typed schema, fits three rating models, and derives a momentum metric. It then writes five denormalised tables — one per screen — which a read-only FastAPI service serves to a Next.js front end.
Three pages: a form board, a player page that leads with a claim and backs it with every recent match beside the probability published before it, and a method page.

images.alt: A Baseline player page showing a career rating timeline above a table of recent matches, each with the win probability published before the match
images.caption: A player page: the claim first, then the career timeline, then the per-match evidence.

images.alt: The Baseline method page showing accuracy against official rankings, a calibration curve, and a list of claims the project does not make
images.caption: The method page publishes the out-of-sample record, the calibration curve, and the claims the project explicitly refuses to make.

result: On main-draw matches Baseline is right 69.7% of the time against the official ranking's 67.3%, and is materially better calibrated — 1.5% average error against 5.0%. Both numbers are published on the site itself, next to a list of things the project does not claim: it has not been benchmarked against betting markets and expects to lose that comparison, ratings are not comparable across eras, and nothing it reports is a cause.
technical: The API only ever reads the five product tables. Each one is shaped for exactly one view, so every endpoint is a single filtered read and no analysis runs inside an HTTP handler — which leaves the research schemas free to change without breaking the product.

Three rules hold the API contract together. Coverage travels with the data: every response carries `data_through` and `is_current`, so a page cannot render 19-month-old WTA numbers as if they were live. Momentum is never a bare number, because its population mean is +0.13 rather than 0 and a raw score reads as "hot" when it is average. And absence is typed — a player below the reliability threshold returns `null` with a reason, never a zero.

122 tests run against a small real slice of data checked into the repo, in about a second and with no network. Fifteen further tests assert real-world facts a one-season fixture cannot support; they are marked and reported as deselected rather than passing silently.

The deployable artefact is not the 1.3 GB research warehouse but a 39 MB product-only export, baked into the container image so a deploy is a single immutable thing and a running API can never be missing its data.
